paragraphs: This Bill brings to an end one chapter in the long connection between Britain and India, but it opens another. British rule which has endured so long is now, at the instance of this country, coming to an end.

There have been many instances in history when States at the point of the sword have been forced to surrender government over another people. It is very rare for a people that have long enjoyed power over another nation to surrender it voluntarily. …

It has been the settled policy of all parties in this country for many years that Indians, in course of time, should manage their own affairs. The question has always been how and when? … They have all wanted to maintain the unity of India, to give India complete self-government and to preserve the rights of minorities. Every one of them has hoped that a solution might be found without resorting to partition. I know that many Indians of all communities passionately desire this, but it has not been found to be practicable. We and the Indian statesmen have had to accept the only alternative—partition. …

The demand for self-government has been insistently pressed for many years by the leaders of political thought in India, and has been stimulated by the external situation, and particularly by those great waves of nationalist feeling that accompanied both the great wars. This demand is not peculiar to India, but has spread throughout Asia. … Delay in granting it has always led to more and more extreme demands. …

… In this Bill, we set up two independent Dominions, free and equal, of no less status than the United Kingdom or the Dominion of Canada, completely free in all respects from any control by this country, but united by a common allegiance to the Sovereign and by a community of ideas, receiving from their membership of the Commonwealth great advantages, but in no way suffering any restriction. …

I saw with great regret in one paper, and I think in one paper only, that the action which we are now taking was described as abdication. It is not the abdication, but the fulfilment of Britain's mission in India.

paragraphs: Nonetheless, the key issue—politically, strategically and morally—underlying the security of the "safe areas"* was the essential nature of "ethnic cleansing". As part of the larger ambition for a "Greater Serbia", the Bosnian Serbs set out to occupy the territory of the enclaves; they wanted the territory for themselves. The civilian inhabitants of the enclaves were not the incidental victims of the attackers; their death or removal was the very purpose of the attacks upon them. … The Bosnian Muslim civilian population thus became the principal victim of brutally aggressive military and paramilitary Serb operations to depopulate coveted territories in order to allow them to be repopulated by Serbs. …

The cardinal lesson of Srebrenica is that a deliberate and systematic attempt to terrorize, expel or murder an entire people must be met decisively with all necessary means, and with the political will to carry the policy through to its logical conclusion. In the Balkans, in this decade, this lesson has had to be learned not once, but twice. In both instances, in Bosnia and in Kosovo, the international community tried to reach a negotiated settlement with an unscrupulous and murderous regime. In both instances it required the use of force to bring a halt to the planned and systematic killing and expulsion of civilians.

The United Nations experience in Bosnia was one of the most difficult and painful in our history. It is with the deepest regret and remorse that we have reviewed our own actions and decisions in the face of the assault on Srebrenica. Through error, misjudgement and an inability to recognize the scope of the evil confronting us, we failed to do our part to help save the people of Srebrenica from the Serb campaign of mass murder. …

paragraphs: After the destruction of the Second World War, the nations of Europe struggled to rebuild their economies and ensure their security. The former required a massive influx of aid to help the war-torn landscapes re-establish industries and produce food, and the latter required assurances against a resurgent Germany or incursions from the Soviet Union. The United States viewed an economically strong, rearmed, and integrated Europe as vital to the prevention of communist expansion across the continent. … Soviet refusal either to participate in the Marshall Plan or to allow its satellite states in Eastern Europe to accept the economic assistance helped to reinforce the growing division between east and west in Europe.

In 1947–1948, a series of events caused the nations of Western Europe to become concerned about their physical and political security and the United States to become more closely involved with European affairs. The ongoing civil war in Greece, along with tensions in Turkey, led President Harry S. Truman to assert that the United States would provide economic and military aid to both countries, as well as to any other nation struggling against an attempt at subjugation. A Soviet-sponsored coup in Czechoslovakia resulted in a communist government coming to power on the borders of Germany. Attention also focused on elections in Italy as the communist party had made significant gains among Italian voters. …

… In 1952, the members agreed to admit Greece and Turkey to NATO and added the Federal Republic of Germany in 1955. West German entry led the Soviet Union to retaliate with its own regional alliance, which took the form of the Warsaw Treaty Organization and included the Soviet satellite states of Eastern Europe as members.
The collective defense arrangements in NATO served to place the whole of Western Europe under the American "nuclear umbrella."* …

paragraphs: My Lords, 1978 saw the birth in this country of a child described as the world's first test-tube baby.* For some couples this was a major breakthrough because it offered the only method by which they might have a child which would be genetically their own. Alongside the wonder this caused and the hopes it raised, there grew understandable concern and some disquiet about where this new technology might lead. There then also grew a belief that the issues were wider than those of medical ethics; so wide, in fact, that they should be subject to the scrutiny of society as a whole. So it was that in 1982 the Government established this inquiry whose report is before us today. …
… It was chaired by Dame Mary Warnock, and its membership reflected a wide range of lay, professional and religious interests. …

… I will highlight only the key proposals. These are, that there should be a statutory body to license and inspect all infertility services where the new techniques are used, and the use of human embryos in research. … In particular, there should be an absolute limit of 14 days after fertilisation after which embryos may not be further developed …

There is no doubt that many of the issues in this report will arouse strong and widely differing opinions. Indeed, among the public at large they are already doing so. There will not be a consensus view on all recommendations. The members of the committee were divided in their view on certain aspects of research and on surrogacy.

paragraphs: It is my privilege to be able to tell the House that a comprehensive political agreement was reached late in the afternoon of 10 April—Good Friday. …

This is a unique agreement born of a unique set of negotiations that involved Unionists, nationalists, republicans and loyalists around the same talks table. This is a situation in which, although compromises have been made, everyone can be a winner. Everyone's political and cultural identity is respected and protected by this deal. Northern Ireland politics, for so long, has been seen as a zero sum game. …

It is important, when we are talking about all the positive developments, that at the same time we do not lose sight of the terrible price that has been paid by the victims of violence and their families. …

The main elements in the agreement are as follows. First, on constitutional issues, the British and Irish Governments have formally resolved our historical differences through the general and future acceptance of the principle of consent, which means that Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom, and will stay that way for as long as that is the wish of a majority of people who live there; and it means that, if the people of Northern Ireland were formally to consent to the establishment of a united Ireland, the Government of the day would bring forward proposals, in consultation with the Irish Government, to give effect to that wish. …

The second part of the agreement says that there will be greater democratic accountability in Northern Ireland through the devolution of a wide range of executive and legislative powers to a Northern Ireland assembly. In the assembly, the posts of executive authority will be shared out on a proportional basis, and safeguards will be in place to protect the interests of both the communities. …

practice.stem: The reforms that Gorbachev describes, such as perestroika and glasnost, were most directly a response to which of the following?

options.A: the Hungarian Revolution of 1956
options.B: the oil price shocks of 1973 and 1979
options.C: long-term Soviet economic stagnation
options.D: demands for reform from the communist leaders of Eastern Europe

practice.explanation: By the late 1970s the Soviet economy grew very slowly. Factories were out of date, and stores often ran short of goods. Gorbachev became leader in 1985. He began perestroika ("restructuring") and glasnost ("openness") to make the system work better.

whyNot.A: The Hungarian Revolution came in 1956, more than thirty years before this speech, and Soviet troops crushed it. Gorbachev's reforms answered problems inside the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s.
whyNot.B: The oil price rises of 1973 and 1979 hurt Western Europe. The Soviet Union sold oil abroad, so for a time it earned more money.
whyNot.D: Most communist leaders in Eastern Europe, such as East Germany's Erich Honecker, disliked Gorbachev's reforms. The reforms answered problems inside the Soviet Union itself.

practice.hint: Gorbachev took power in 1985. What had been happening to the Soviet economy in the years before that?

practice.stem: Which of the following later developments would best support the argument that Gorbachev put his principle of "freedom of choice" into practice?

options.A: Soviet troops attacked independence protesters in Lithuania in 1991.
options.B: The Soviet Union let Solidarity lead Poland's government in 1989.
options.C: China's army crushed student protests in Tiananmen Square in 1989.
options.D: Yugoslavia broke apart in a series of wars beginning in 1991.

practice.explanation: In June 1989 Poland held partly free elections. Solidarity won almost every seat it was allowed to run for. Gorbachev did not send troops. In August 1989 Tadeusz Mazowiecki of Solidarity became prime minister.

whyNot.A: Using troops against Lithuanians who wanted independence went against freedom of choice. It would challenge the argument, not support it.
whyNot.C: China was outside Soviet control. So this event does not show whether Gorbachev let the Soviet Union's allies choose their own governments.
whyNot.D: Yugoslavia was a communist country outside the Soviet bloc. Its wars grew out of conflict among its own peoples, not out of a Soviet decision.

practice.hint: Which choices are about a country in the Soviet bloc? What did the Soviet Union do there?

practice.stem: Gorbachev most likely announced the troop cuts described in the last two paragraphs at the United Nations in order to

options.A: warn NATO that Soviet forces would defend the Warsaw Pact countries
options.B: persuade the United States to pull its troops out of West Germany first
options.C: show the West that the Soviet Union wanted to end the arms race
options.D: prepare the way for German reunification under a communist government

practice.explanation: Gorbachev spoke to the whole world at the UN. By cutting 500,000 troops without asking for anything in return, he tried to show Western leaders that the Soviet Union wanted to end the arms race. The cuts would also save money for the weak Soviet economy.

whyNot.A: Gorbachev is pulling six tank divisions out of East Germany, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary. That weakens Soviet forces there instead of threatening NATO.
whyNot.B: Gorbachev says the cuts "will be done unilaterally," without waiting for the United States to act.
whyNot.D: Gorbachev does not mention German unity. When Germany reunited in 1990, East Germany joined West Germany's democratic system.

practice.hint: Who was listening to a speech at the United Nations, and what did Gorbachev give up without asking for anything in return?

practice.stem: The idea that "all peoples have the right to self-determination" is most similar to the ideas of which leader at the Paris Peace Conference of 1919?

options.A: Georges Clemenceau
options.B: David Lloyd George
options.C: Woodrow Wilson
options.D: Vittorio Orlando

practice.explanation: In 1918 U.S. President Woodrow Wilson called for self-determination, the right of peoples to choose their own governments. His Fourteen Points and other speeches raised hopes in colonies. In 1919 the idea was applied mostly in Europe, for new states such as Poland and Czechoslovakia. Many colonies in Asia and Africa had to wait until after 1945.

whyNot.A: France's leader, Georges Clemenceau, wanted to punish Germany and protect France. France kept its empire and gained new lands as League of Nations mandates.
whyNot.B: Britain's leader, David Lloyd George, worked to keep the British Empire together. Britain also gained new lands as mandates.
whyNot.D: Italy's leader, Vittorio Orlando, wanted the lands that the Allies had promised Italy in 1915, even where most people were not Italian.

practice.hint: Which leader's peace plan of 1918 raised hopes in colonies around the world?

practice.stem: When the declaration was adopted, its demand that "all armed action or repressive measures" against dependent peoples "shall cease" applied most directly to which conflict then under way?

options.A: the Irish War of Independence
options.B: the Spanish Civil War
options.C: the Soviet Union's war in Afghanistan
options.D: the Algerian War of Independence

practice.explanation: France fought Algeria's National Liberation Front (FLN) from 1954 to 1962. French forces used harsh methods, including torture. When the UN voted in December 1960, the war was still going on, and France abstained. Algeria became independent in 1962.

whyNot.A: Ireland fought Britain for independence from 1919 to 1921, almost forty years before this declaration.
whyNot.B: The Spanish Civil War (1936 to 1939) was a fight over who would rule Spain, not a colony's fight against a colonial power. It had ended long before 1960.
whyNot.C: The Soviet war in Afghanistan began in 1979, almost twenty years after this declaration.

practice.hint: Check the dates. Which of these wars was going on in December 1960?

practice.stem: The declaration's call to "transfer all powers to the peoples" of colonies "without any conditions or reservations" was carried out for Portugal's African colonies most directly as a result of which of the following?

options.A: the 1974 revolution in Portugal
options.B: the Suez Crisis of 1956
options.C: Portugal's entry into the European Community
options.D: the end of the Cold War

practice.explanation: Portugal's dictatorship fought long wars against independence movements in Angola (from 1961), Guinea-Bissau, and Mozambique. In April 1974 army officers overthrew the dictatorship in the Carnation Revolution. The new government gave the colonies independence in 1974 and 1975.

whyNot.B: The Suez Crisis of 1956 came before this declaration. It weakened Britain and France, but Portugal held on to its African colonies for almost twenty more years.
whyNot.C: Portugal joined the European Community in 1986. By then its African colonies had been independent for more than ten years.
whyNot.D: The Cold War ended between 1989 and 1991. Portugal's African colonies had become independent in 1974 and 1975.

practice.hint: When did Portugal's African colonies become independent? Look for the event that came just before.

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Bevan wants more hospitals run by private charities, while Howe wants the government to build a national health service.
options.B: Bevan blames the war for Britain's poor health, while Howe blames the war for Britain's slow economic growth.
options.C: Bevan wants the state to give free health care to all, while Howe wants lower taxes and a smaller state.
options.D: Bevan wants local councils to run the economy, while Howe wants the national government to plan it.

practice.explanation: Bevan wanted a universal health service, free to everyone and paid for by the public. Howe argued that high taxes and a large state were holding Britain back and that the state's role should shrink.

whyNot.A: Bevan says it is "repugnant" for hospitals to rely on private charity. Howe does not call for a new health service.
whyNot.B: Bevan argues that cost keeps people from seeking care; he does not blame the war. Howe blames taxes and government interference for weak economic growth.
whyNot.D: Howe attacks government planning of the economy. Bevan is talking about health care, not about who runs the economy.

practice.stem: Howe's arguments in Source 2 are best understood in the context of

options.A: economic slowdown and inflation after the oil shocks of the 1970s
options.B: the shortage of workers in Britain caused by the Second World War
options.C: the collapse of communist governments in Eastern Europe
options.D: the mass unemployment of the Great Depression in the 1930s

practice.explanation: Oil prices rose sharply in 1973 and again in 1979. Britain and other Western countries faced stagflation, which means slow growth together with rising prices. Critics blamed high taxes and government spending, and Thatcher's new government promised to cut both.

whyNot.B: Postwar labor shortages were a problem of the late 1940s and 1950s. Howe is speaking in 1979.
whyNot.C: Communist governments in Eastern Europe fell in 1989, ten years after this speech.
whyNot.D: The Great Depression was in the 1930s. Howe is reacting to the problems of the 1970s.

practice.hint: When was this speech given, and what had happened to the world economy in the years before it?

practice.stem: Which of the following best explains the faster growth of France and West Germany that Howe describes?

options.A: industrial investment and expanding trade within the Common Market
options.B: the colonial empires that France and West Germany kept after 1945
options.C: the reparations that Britain paid to France and Germany after the war
options.D: the absence of welfare programs in France and West Germany

practice.explanation: After the war, France and West Germany invested heavily in new factories and machines. The Common Market, created in 1957, lowered trade barriers among its members and gave them a large market for their goods. West Germany's fast growth was called its economic miracle. Britain also received Marshall Plan aid, but it did not join the Common Market until 1973.

whyNot.B: West Germany had no colonies after 1945, and France was losing most of its empire in the 1950s and 1960s.
whyNot.C: Britain paid no reparations. Germany, not Britain, was the defeated power.
whyNot.D: Both France and West Germany built large welfare systems after the war. Their growth came alongside welfare spending.

practice.hint: What helped the economies of France and West Germany recover so quickly after 1945?

practice.stem: Truman's promise of aid described in the second paragraph is best understood as an early example of which U.S. policy?

options.A: détente
options.B: containment
options.C: appeasement
options.D: isolationism

practice.explanation: In March 1947 Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey. This became known as the Truman Doctrine. It began the U.S. policy of containment, which aimed to stop the spread of communism.

whyNot.A: Détente was the easing of tension between the superpowers in the 1970s. Truman was promising aid to resist communism in 1947.
whyNot.C: Appeasement was the British and French policy of giving in to Hitler in the 1930s. Truman promised to help nations resist, not give in.
whyNot.D: Isolationism meant staying out of Europe's affairs. The passage says the United States became "more closely involved with European affairs."

practice.hint: According to the first paragraph, what did the United States want to prevent?

practice.stem: Which of the following provides the best evidence for the historians' claim that the Soviet Union would not "allow its satellite states in Eastern Europe to accept the economic assistance"?

options.A: Communist parties in several European states joined the Soviet-backed Cominform in 1947.
options.B: The Soviet Union supported the communist takeover of Czechoslovakia in 1948.
options.C: The Soviet Union set up COMECON to coordinate Eastern European economies in 1949.
options.D: Czechoslovakia and Poland refused Marshall Plan aid in 1947 under Soviet pressure.

practice.explanation: In July 1947 Czechoslovakia agreed to attend the Paris talks on the Marshall Plan. Then Stalin called its leaders to Moscow, and they pulled out. Poland also turned down the aid under Soviet pressure.

whyNot.A: The Cominform linked communist parties to Moscow. Its founding does not directly show that the satellites were kept from taking Marshall Plan aid.
whyNot.B: The takeover shows Soviet power over Czechoslovakia. But it is not about whether the country could accept Marshall Plan aid.
whyNot.C: COMECON was the Soviet answer to the Marshall Plan. But it does not directly show that the satellites were stopped from taking the aid.

practice.hint: The claim is about whether the satellites could accept economic aid. Which choice is directly about that?

practice.stem: The "nuclear umbrella" described in the last paragraph contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: the Berlin Airlift
options.B: the European Coal and Steel Community
options.C: the Hungarian Revolution of 1956
options.D: the nuclear arms race

practice.explanation: The United States promised to defend Western Europe with nuclear weapons. The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949. Both sides then built more and more powerful weapons. This arms race raised the threat of nuclear war for decades.

whyNot.A: The Berlin Airlift began in 1948, before NATO existed. It answered the Soviet blockade of West Berlin.
whyNot.B: The European Coal and Steel Community (1951) joined the coal and steel industries of six countries. It came from plans for economic cooperation, not from nuclear defense.
whyNot.C: Hungarians rose against Soviet control in 1956. The revolt was not caused by NATO's nuclear umbrella.

practice.hint: If one side relies on nuclear weapons to protect its allies, how is the other side likely to respond?
