options.C: West German payments to the victims of the Holocaust
options.D: U.S. loans to Germany under the Dawes Plan

practice.explanation: The Marshall Plan (1948–1952) sent billions of dollars in American aid to Western Europe. West Berlin got some of it. The money helped rebuild industry, housing, and businesses after the war.

whyNot.A: The Kurfürstendamm is in West Berlin, and the sign names the Marshall Plan, an American program. The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid.
whyNot.C: In 1952 West Germany did agree to pay Israel and Jewish groups. But that money did not build hotels in Berlin.
whyNot.D: The Dawes Plan of 1924 lent American money to Germany so it could pay reparations after World War I. The sign names the Marshall Plan, which began in 1948.

practice.hint: Look at the date of the photograph and the program named on the sign.

practice.stem: Given its context, Zentralbild most likely released the photograph and its caption in order to

options.A: portray American aid as serving the rich instead of ordinary Berliners
options.B: thank the United States for helping to rebuild both halves of the divided city of Berlin
options.C: encourage East Germans to cross into West Berlin to take jobs on its building sites
options.D: show that East Germany had also received aid from the Marshall Plan

practice.explanation: Both sides used propaganda in the Cold War. Zentralbild used this photo to attack the Marshall Plan. Its caption said the money built hotels and banks while some people still lived in huts.

whyNot.B: Zentralbild worked in East Germany, whose government was allied with the Soviet Union and opposed the Marshall Plan. Its caption attacks the aid instead of thanking anyone.
whyNot.C: East Germany wanted to stop its people from leaving for the West, not encourage them to work there.
whyNot.D: East Germany received no Marshall Plan aid. The Soviet Union refused it for the whole Soviet bloc.

practice.hint: Who sent out this photograph, and which side of the Cold War were they on?

practice.stem: The Soviet Union responded to programs like the one named on the sign by

options.A: joining the European Coal and Steel Community
options.B: accepting Marshall Plan aid for East Berlin
options.C: giving up its control over East German industry
options.D: creating the COMECON trading bloc

practice.explanation: The Soviet Union turned down Marshall Plan aid. It made the Eastern European countries turn it down too. In 1949 it set up COMECON to tie their economies to its own.

whyNot.A: The European Coal and Steel Community (1951) joined France, West Germany, Italy, and the Benelux countries. No communist state joined it.
whyNot.B: The Soviet Union refused all Marshall Plan aid, including for its zone of Germany and East Berlin.
whyNot.C: The Soviet Union kept tight control over East Germany's economy. It had also taken factories and machines from its zone as payment for war damage.

practice.hint: Recall how the Soviet Union treated the Marshall Plan in 1947–1949.

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Nagy asks for more Soviet troops to restore order, while Kádár demands that the Soviet troops leave Hungary.
options.B: Nagy asks the UN to defend Hungary's neutrality, while Kádár says the UN has no right to discuss Hungary.
options.C: Nagy wants Hungary to stay in the Warsaw Pact, while Kádár wants Hungary to leave the alliance and be neutral.
options.D: Nagy speaks for a government in exile, while Kádár speaks for Hungary's elected parliament.

practice.explanation: Nagy declared Hungary neutral and pulled out of the Warsaw Pact. He asked the UN and the great powers to protect Hungary. Three days later, Kádár's new government told the UN to stay out. It said the matter was Hungary's business alone.

whyNot.A: Nagy protests the entry of Soviet troops and demands their withdrawal. Kádár does not ask the Soviet troops to leave.
whyNot.C: Nagy says Hungary "repudiates the Warsaw Treaty." Kádár's government kept Hungary in the Warsaw Pact.
whyNot.D: Nagy was in Budapest as prime minister when he sent his telegram. Kádár's government was not elected; it was set up with Soviet backing.

practice.hint: What does each telegram ask the United Nations to do?

practice.stem: A historian should be cautious about accepting Kádár's claim that Nagy's requests did not come from "Hungary as a State" mainly because

options.A: Kádár's government faced economic shortages after the fighting
options.B: Kádár's government claimed that Hungary controlled its own internal affairs
options.C: Kádár's government included officials who had also served under Nagy
options.D: Kádár's government depended on the Soviet attack that had just pushed Nagy aside

practice.explanation: On November 4, 1956, Soviet tanks attacked Budapest, and Kádár announced a new government backed by the Soviet Union. His telegram served Soviet aims by trying to keep the UN from acting. Nagy was later arrested and executed in 1958.

whyNot.A: Shortages do not explain why Kádár would deny that Nagy spoke for Hungary.
whyNot.B: This repeats Kádár's own claim. It does not explain why a historian should doubt it.
whyNot.C: Sharing some officials with Nagy's government does not make Kádár's claim more or less believable. What matters most is that his government owed its power to the Soviet attack.

practice.hint: Think about how Kádár came to power and what his government needed from the world.

practice.stem: Which of the following best explains why Western governments did not send troops to help Nagy's government?

options.A: The UN Security Council had voted to approve the Soviet army's action in Hungary as lawful self-defense.
options.B: They feared that fighting in the Soviet bloc could start a nuclear war with the Soviet Union.
options.C: Hungary had refused to accept help from Western countries.
options.D: The United States and Britain had no troops stationed in Europe in 1956.

practice.explanation: The UN General Assembly condemned the Soviet attack, but the United States and its allies did not send troops. They treated Hungary as part of the Soviet sphere and feared a nuclear war. Britain and France were also busy with their invasion of Egypt in the Suez Crisis.

whyNot.A: The Soviet Union used its veto to block action in the Security Council. Then the General Assembly condemned the Soviet attack.
whyNot.C: Nagy asked the UN and the great powers for help in defending Hungary's neutrality.
whyNot.D: American and British troops were stationed in West Germany as part of NATO in 1956.

practice.hint: What did both superpowers have by 1956 that made a direct war so dangerous?

practice.stem: Which conclusion about the period from 1965 to 1990 is best supported by the data?

options.A: Most of the countries shown had lower rates in 1990 than in 1965.
options.B: Rates in the communist countries fell faster than rates in the Western countries.
options.C: Italy's rate rose while the rates of the other countries fell.
options.D: Ireland's rate stayed about the same throughout the period.

practice.explanation: Six of the seven countries had lower rates in 1990 than in 1965. Only Hungary's rose slightly. The postwar baby boom was over.

whyNot.B: Hungary's rate rose from 1.82 to 1.87, and Poland's fell by less than half a child. Italy's fell by more than one child.
whyNot.C: Italy's rate fell from 2.60 to 1.33, one of the largest drops in the table.
whyNot.D: Ireland's rate fell by almost half, from 4.04 to 2.11.

practice.hint: Compare the 1965 and 1990 columns row by row.

practice.stem: Which type of government policy would most likely help explain Hungary's different trend between 1965 and 1975?

options.A: expanding access to contraception through public health services
options.B: encouraging longer periods of education before marriage
options.C: increasing family payments while limiting access to abortion
options.D: reducing paid leave for parents of young children

practice.explanation: Communist Hungary worried about its low birth rate. From 1967 it paid mothers an allowance to stay home with young children. In 1973 it decided to limit abortion, starting in January 1974, and it raised family payments. Births rose for a few years. Policies like these, meant to raise the birth rate, are called pronatalist.

whyNot.A: Easier access to birth control makes it easier to avoid or delay having children. It would not raise the rate.
whyNot.B: Staying in school longer before marriage usually delays having children.
whyNot.D: Less paid leave would make caring for young children harder for working parents. It would not encourage more births.

practice.hint: Hungary's rate went up while most others went down. Would each policy make people more likely or less likely to have children?

practice.stem: The overall trend in the table after 1965 was most directly influenced by

options.A: the deaths of millions of young men in the Second World War
options.B: the birth control pill and women's growing paid work
options.C: government bans on contraception across Western Europe
options.D: the arrival of migrant families with many children

practice.explanation: The birth control pill became available in many European countries in the 1960s. More women stayed in school and took paid jobs. Couples chose to have fewer children. Birth rates fell well below the baby-boom levels of the early 1960s.

whyNot.A: World War II ended in 1945, long before most of the fall shown in the table. Birth rates rose after the war in the baby boom.
whyNot.C: Contraception became easier to get after 1960. France legalized the pill in 1967 and Britain offered it from 1961.
whyNot.D: Families with many children could not explain a fall in the number of children born per woman. Children born abroad are not counted in a country's rate.

practice.hint: Check the dates. Which choice describes a change that began in the 1960s and would lead to fewer births?

practice.stem: According to the Court, one aim of Article 119 was to

options.A: allow each member state to set its own rules on how much women should be paid
options.B: protect firms in equal-pay states from rivals that paid women less
options.C: protect women from working in dangerous jobs such as flying on airplanes
options.D: encourage women to leave paid work and stay home to raise children

practice.explanation: The Court gave two aims. The economic aim was fair competition: firms in states that paid women equally should not lose out to firms in states that did not. The social aim was to improve living and working conditions.

whyNot.A: The Court says equal pay is part of "the foundations of the Community." So Article 119 set a common rule. States still made their own pay laws, but those laws had to respect equal pay.
whyNot.C: The case is about a flight attendant who was paid less than men doing the same work. It is not about keeping women out of jobs.
whyNot.D: The Court says Article 119 aims at "social progress" for workers. It does not tell women to leave paid work.

practice.hint: Reread the paragraph that begins "First."

practice.stem: The Defrenne case is best understood in the context of

options.A: women's campaigns of the 1960s and 1970s for equal pay at work
options.B: women winning the right to vote in most Western European countries for the first time
options.C: government efforts to send women home from factory jobs after World War II
options.D: the closing of universities to women in Western Europe

practice.explanation: In the 1960s and 1970s, feminists pushed for equal pay. In 1966 thousands of women at a factory in Herstal, Belgium, went on strike for equal pay. In 1968 women at a Ford factory in Dagenham, England, did the same.

whyNot.B: Most Western European women had won the vote between 1918 and 1948, well before this case.
whyNot.C: Some women were pushed out of factory jobs in 1945, but this case was decided in 1976 and was about equal pay.
whyNot.D: Universities in Western Europe were open to women. The number of women students grew fast after 1960.

practice.hint: What were women's groups demanding in the years when Defrenne brought her case?

practice.stem: The ruling best illustrates which challenge that membership in the European Community posed to its member states?

options.A: National courts could no longer apply Community law in cases against private employers.
options.B: Community law could force changes even where national laws lagged behind.
options.C: Member states had to bring wages to one level across the Community.
options.D: Member states had to let the Court of Justice write their labor laws.

practice.explanation: The Court said workers could use Article 119 in their own national courts. They could do so even before national laws changed. So Community law could override national rules. Some people saw this as a threat to national sovereignty.

whyNot.A: The ruling did the opposite. Workers could now use the equal-pay rule in their own national courts, even against private employers.
whyNot.C: The ruling was about equal pay for women and men doing the same work. It did not make wages the same in every member state.
whyNot.D: Member states still wrote their own labor laws. Those laws had to respect the equal-pay rule.

practice.hint: What does the last paragraph say about the "resistance" of some member states?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes Glenarthur's main point?

options.A: Doctors, not Parliament, should decide how new fertility treatments are used.
options.B: The Warnock committee's members agreed about surrogacy and embryo research.
options.C: New fertility techniques raised moral questions that called for debate and legal rules.
options.D: The government planned to ban fertility treatment and embryo research in Britain.

practice.explanation: The birth of the first "test-tube baby" in 1978 raised hopes and fears. Glenarthur explains that the government set up an inquiry. The inquiry proposed rules set by law. People strongly disagreed about some of the issues.

whyNot.A: Glenarthur says the issues were "wider than those of medical ethics." He says "society as a whole" should examine them.
whyNot.B: He says the committee's members "were divided" on research and surrogacy.
whyNot.D: The proposals would license fertility services, not ban them.

practice.hint: What does Glenarthur say about who should examine these issues, and about whether people agree?

practice.stem: The proposals described in the passage most directly led to which of the following?

options.A: a 1990 law creating an authority to license fertility clinics
options.B: a 1985 law that banned research on human embryos
options.C: a European Union law requiring member states to allow surrogacy
options.D: the Catholic Church's approval of in vitro fertilisation

practice.explanation: In 1990 Parliament passed the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act. It set up an authority to license fertility clinics and embryo research. The law kept the 14-day limit that the Warnock Report proposed.

whyNot.B: In 1985 Enoch Powell's bill to ban embryo research won a large vote in the House of Commons, but it ran out of time and never became law. The 1990 act allowed research up to 14 days.
whyNot.C: The European Union has left surrogacy to its member states, and many of them forbid it.
whyNot.D: The Catholic Church spoke out against IVF in 1987. It still opposes it.

practice.hint: Find the choice that fits the report's proposals, then check whether the date and the details are right.

practice.stem: Technologies like the one described in the passage most directly affected women's lives by

options.A: lowering the age at which most women had their first child
options.B: making large families common again in Western Europe
options.C: giving some women more choices about motherhood
options.D: reducing the number of women who took paid jobs

practice.explanation: IVF and other new methods let some women who could not conceive have children. With the birth control pill, these tools gave women more choices about motherhood. They also caused moral debates.

whyNot.A: Women in Britain had their first child at older ages after the 1970s, not younger. IVF helped some older women become mothers.
whyNot.B: Families stayed small. Birth rates in Western Europe stayed low in the 1980s and 1990s.
whyNot.D: More British women took paid jobs in the 1980s, not fewer.

practice.hint: What did the new technique offer couples who could not have children?

practice.stem: The declaration is best understood in the context of

options.A: the rise of anti-immigrant parties such as France's National Front
options.B: the arrival of large numbers of refugees from the wars in Yugoslavia
options.C: the end of colonial empires, which stopped migration from Africa and Asia
options.D: the Soviet Union's decision to let its citizens move freely to Western Europe

practice.explanation: After the slowdown of the 1970s, many immigrants faced hatred. In 1984 France's anti-immigrant National Front won about 11 percent of the vote in the European elections. European leaders made this statement to condemn racism.

whyNot.B: The wars in Yugoslavia began in 1991, five years after this declaration.
whyNot.C: The end of empire led to more migration to Europe from former colonies, not less.
whyNot.D: The Soviet Union still kept tight limits on emigration in 1986. The limits eased only in the late 1980s.

practice.hint: The declaration speaks of the "growth of xenophobic attitudes, movements." What movements were growing in the 1980s?

practice.stem: The workers who had their "origins … in third countries" most likely included

options.A: Italians who moved to West Germany to take industrial jobs
options.B: East Germans who had moved to the West after the Berlin Wall opened
options.C: Soviet soldiers stationed in East Germany under the Warsaw Pact
options.D: Turks and North Africans recruited to fill jobs during the boom of the 1960s

practice.explanation: West Germany signed deals to recruit workers from Turkey (1961), Morocco (1963), and Tunisia (1965). France drew many workers from Algeria and Morocco. Many stayed and brought their families. In 1986 none of these four countries belonged to the Community.

whyNot.A: Italy was a founding member of the European Community. Italian workers came from another member state, not from a "third country."
whyNot.B: The Berlin Wall opened in 1989, three years after this declaration. East Germans were also not foreigners under West German law.
whyNot.C: These soldiers were troops sent by their government, not workers who had moved for jobs. Also, East Germany was not in the European Community.

practice.hint: "Third countries" are countries outside the Community. Who came from outside to work in Western Europe during the boom years?

practice.stem: The declaration's claim that rejecting racial discrimination is part of "the common cultural and legal heritage of all the Member States" is best understood as part of an effort to

options.A: limit immigration into the Community to people of European descent
options.B: replace the national governments with a single European government
options.C: define a shared European identity based on human rights
options.D: revive the nationalist ideas of nineteenth-century Europe

practice.explanation: After World War II and the Holocaust, European leaders called human rights a shared European value. This declaration says that respecting people of every background is part of being European.

whyNot.A: The declaration condemns hostility based on "racial, religious, cultural, social or national differences." It does not call for limits based on descent.
whyNot.B: Representatives of the member states signed the declaration. The states stayed in charge of their own countries.
whyNot.D: Nineteenth-century nationalism stressed loyalty to one nation. The declaration stresses values that the member states share.

practice.hint: What does the declaration say all the member states have in common?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Economic growth should stop until the pollution of the past has been cleaned up.
options.B: Each member state should deal with pollution on its own, without common rules.
options.C: Protecting nature matters less than raising standards of living as fast as possible.
options.D: Economic growth should raise the quality of life, so pollution must be fought together.

practice.explanation: The programme says that growth is not a goal in itself. It should improve the quality of life, protect the environment, make polluters pay, and be planned together by the member states.

whyNot.A: The leaders say expansion "should result in an improvement in the quality of life as well as in standards of living." They do not call for growth to stop.
whyNot.B: Principle 11 says these policies "must no longer be planned and implemented in isolation." States should work together.
whyNot.C: The leaders say "economic expansion is not an end in itself" and that the environment must be protected.

practice.hint: What do the leaders say economic expansion should lead to?

practice.stem: In the following decades, ideas like those in the passage were taken up most strongly by which of the following?

options.A: Free-market conservative parties
options.B: Green parties
options.C: Communist parties of Eastern Europe
options.D: Anti-immigrant nationalist parties

practice.explanation: Green parties began to form in the 1970s and grew stronger in the 1980s. West Germany's Greens first won seats in its parliament in 1983. They criticized consumerism and fought to protect the environment.

whyNot.A: Free-market conservatives such as Thatcher's Conservatives stressed growth, lower taxes, and fewer rules on business. The environment was not their main cause.
whyNot.C: Communist governments in Eastern Europe built heavy industry and caused terrible pollution. Acid rain hurt forests in Czechoslovakia and Poland.
whyNot.D: Anti-immigrant parties cared most about stopping immigration. Protecting nature was not their main goal.

practice.hint: Compare each party's main concern with the main concern of the passage.

practice.stem: Which demand of many European student protesters in 1968 most closely resembled the argument of the passage?

options.A: less focus on consumer goods and more personal freedom
options.B: stronger executive leadership and greater national prestige
options.C: making polluters pay the cost of the harm they cause
options.D: faster economic growth through closer European trade ties

practice.explanation: In 1968 students protested in France, West Germany, Italy, and other countries. Many attacked the consumer society and old-fashioned authority. Like the passage, they asked whether making and buying more goods really made life better.

whyNot.B: In France the students protested against President de Gaulle's strong rule. Strong leadership and national prestige were de Gaulle's goals, not theirs.
whyNot.C: The passage does say polluters should pay. But this rule came from governments in the early 1970s; for example, a group of mostly wealthy countries called the OECD adopted it in 1972. It was not a main demand of the student protesters of 1968.
whyNot.D: This makes faster growth the main goal. The passage warns against judging growth "from purely quantitative aspects."

practice.hint: What did the young protesters of 1968 criticize about the societies built after the war?

practice.stem: The requirement in Article 4 is best understood in the context of

options.A: worry that American films and TV shows were crowding out European ones
options.B: Soviet attempts to block Western radio and television broadcasts to Eastern Europe
options.C: a shortage of television sets in Western European homes
options.D: the decline in movie attendance caused by the spread of radio

practice.explanation: After World War II, American movies, music, and TV shows became very popular in Europe. Many Europeans liked them. Others, especially in France, feared for Europe's own culture. The rule about "European works" was one answer.

whyNot.B: The Soviet bloc did block Western radio. But the directive covers broadcasters inside the European Community.
whyNot.C: By 1989 almost every home in Western Europe had a TV.
whyNot.D: Radio spread in the 1920s and 1930s. The directive deals with television in 1989.

practice.hint: Whose films and shows were Europeans watching most, besides their own?

practice.stem: The directive's statement about "broadcasts transmitted across frontiers by means of various technologies" most directly reflects

options.A: the invention of radio in the 1890s
options.B: the arrival of the internet in most European homes
options.C: satellite and cable television in the 1980s
options.D: the first public television broadcasts in the 1930s

practice.explanation: Satellite and cable television spread quickly in the 1980s. More people could watch channels from other countries. So the Community wanted common rules for broadcasts that crossed borders.

whyNot.A: Radio was invented in the 1890s. That was almost a hundred years before this directive about TV.
whyNot.B: Most European homes went online only in the late 1990s and 2000s, after this 1989 directive.
whyNot.D: Television began in the 1930s, but early stations reached only nearby viewers. The directive answers the later spread of satellite and cable TV.

practice.hint: Check the date of the directive. Which technology was spreading across Europe at that time?

practice.stem: Taken together, Articles 2 and 4 best illustrate the European Community's effort to

options.A: allow each member state to block programs broadcast from other member states
options.B: open a single market in broadcasting while protecting European culture
options.C: ban American programs from European television
options.D: replace national television stations with one European network

practice.explanation: Article 2 lets broadcasts from other member states be received freely. That helps create a single market. Article 4 asks broadcasters to show mostly European works. It protects European culture without banning foreign shows.

whyNot.A: Article 2 says member states "shall not restrict retransmission" of broadcasts from other member states.
whyNot.C: Article 4 asks for a majority of European works "where practicable." American programs could still fill the rest.
whyNot.D: The directive regulates broadcasters in each member state. It does not create one European network.

practice.hint: One article removes barriers between members. What does the other one protect?

practice.stem: The treaty is best understood in the context of

options.A: the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia to end the Prague Spring
options.B: the Berlin Airlift, which kept West Berlin supplied
options.C: the collapse of East Germany's communist government in 1989
options.D: the founding of the European Coal and Steel Community

practice.explanation: The Berlin Wall opened on November 9, 1989, and East Germany's communist government soon fell. East Germans voted in free elections in March 1990. Then the two German states and the four wartime Allies agreed on reunification, which came on October 3, 1990.

whyNot.A: The invasion of Czechoslovakia was in 1968. It strengthened Soviet control instead of ending the division of Europe.
whyNot.B: The Berlin Airlift was in 1948–1949, at the start of the Cold War.
whyNot.D: The European Coal and Steel Community was founded in 1951. It included West Germany but not East Germany.

practice.hint: The treaty speaks of "recent historic changes" that "overcome the division of the continent." What were they?

practice.stem: Article 1's statements about Germany's borders settled a question left open since

options.A: the Treaty of Versailles, when the Rhineland was taken from Germany and given to France
options.B: the Congress of Vienna, when the German Confederation was created
options.C: the Munich Agreement, when Germany took the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia
options.D: the end of World War II, when Poland's border was moved west to the Oder and Neisse rivers

practice.explanation: At Potsdam in 1945, the Allies put German lands east of the Oder and Neisse rivers under Polish control. The final border was left for a later peace treaty. West Germany accepted the line in 1970, but the final settlement came only in 1990.

whyNot.A: The Treaty of Versailles demilitarized the Rhineland but left it part of Germany. It gave Alsace-Lorraine to France.
whyNot.B: The German Confederation of 1815 ended in 1866. The treaty deals with borders drawn after 1945.
whyNot.C: The Munich Agreement of 1938 was undone in 1945. The Sudetenland went back to Czechoslovakia then.

practice.hint: Article 1 mentions Poland. When had Poland's border with Germany been moved, and by whom?

practice.stem: After reunification, Germany used the right recognized in Article 6 by choosing to

options.A: remain a member of NATO
options.B: join the Warsaw Pact
options.C: become a neutral state outside both alliances
options.D: leave the European Community

practice.explanation: West Germany had belonged to NATO since 1955. In July 1990 Gorbachev agreed that a united Germany could choose its own alliances, and it stayed in NATO.

whyNot.B: The Warsaw Pact was the Soviet alliance. Germany stayed in NATO, and the Warsaw Pact itself broke up in 1991.
whyNot.C: The Soviet Union at first wanted a united Germany to be neutral. Germany chose to stay in NATO instead.
whyNot.D: Article 6 is about military alliances. The united Germany stayed a leading member of the European Community.

practice.hint: What did the Soviet Union most fear about a united Germany, and what did it finally accept in 1990?

practice.stem: The "short-sighted policy of the centre" that the leaders blame most likely refers to

options.A: Stalin's collectivization of farms
options.B: the Marshall Plan
options.C: Khrushchev's de-Stalinization
options.D: Gorbachev's perestroika

practice.explanation: Gorbachev's reforms, called perestroika, loosened central planning. But they did not create working markets. Goods ran short, and factories made less. People in the republics blamed the government in Moscow.

whyNot.A: Collectivization was sixty years earlier. The leaders describe a crisis happening now, in 1991.
whyNot.B: The Marshall Plan was an American program. "The centre" means the Soviet government in Moscow.
whyNot.C: Khrushchev began de-Stalinization in 1956, thirty-five years earlier. The leaders describe a crisis of their own time.

practice.hint: The leaders describe a crisis of their own time. Which choice fits the years just before 1991?

practice.stem: Which of the following most directly contributed to the "withdrawal of republics" that the declaration describes?

options.A: the Hungarian Revolution against Soviet control in 1956
options.B: the reunification of East and West Germany in 1990
options.C: the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962
options.D: the failed coup against Gorbachev in August 1991

practice.explanation: In August 1991 hard-line communists tried to remove Gorbachev. The coup failed within three days. Boris Yeltsin led the resistance in Moscow. In the next days and weeks, Ukraine, Belarus, and other republics declared independence.

whyNot.A: Soviet troops crushed the Hungarian Revolution. The Soviet Union then stayed together for 35 more years.
whyNot.B: German reunification ended the division of Germany. It did not make Soviet republics leave the Union.
whyNot.C: The Cuban Missile Crisis was a confrontation with the United States. It did not lead republics to leave the Soviet Union.

practice.hint: What happened in Moscow a few months before this declaration?

practice.stem: The "conflicts between nationalities" that the declaration mentions continued after 1991, most notably in

options.A: the Troubles in Northern Ireland
options.B: the Basque separatist campaign in Spain
options.C: Russia's wars with separatists in Chechnya
options.D: the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina

practice.explanation: Chechnya, a region inside Russia, declared independence in 1991. Russia fought wars there from 1994 to 1996 and again from 1999. Many civilians died. Other conflicts broke out in Georgia, in Moldova, and between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

whyNot.A: The Troubles were in Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom, not the former Soviet Union.
whyNot.B: The Basque campaign was in Spain and France, not the former Soviet Union.
whyNot.D: Bosnia was part of Yugoslavia, not the Soviet Union.

practice.hint: Which of these conflicts took place in a part of the former Soviet Union?

practice.stem: The regulation is best understood in the context of

options.A: the Marshall Plan
options.B: the European Coal and Steel Community
options.C: the Maastricht Treaty
options.D: the breakup of the Soviet ruble zone

practice.explanation: The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 set a timetable for a shared currency. In 1998 eleven member states met its conditions. They adopted the euro on January 1, 1999. Euro notes and coins followed in 2002.

whyNot.A: The Marshall Plan ended in 1952 and created no currency. It did push European countries to work together.
whyNot.B: The Coal and Steel Community of 1951 pooled coal and steel. It did not create a currency.
whyNot.D: Several former Soviet republics kept using the ruble after 1991, until the ruble zone largely broke apart in 1993. The euro was a separate European Union project.

practice.hint: Look at the date of the regulation and its talk of a "third stage." Which choice is closest to it in time and purpose?

practice.stem: The recitals about the United Kingdom and Denmark best illustrate

options.A: the failure of poorer member states to meet the rules for adopting the euro
options.B: some states' wish to keep control of their own currencies
options.C: the expulsion of Britain and Denmark from the European Union
options.D: a plan to make the pound and the krone the EU's shared currencies

practice.explanation: Britain and Denmark won the right to stay out of the single currency in 1992. Many people there saw their own currency as a symbol of national sovereignty. Danish voters rejected the euro in a referendum in 2000.

whyNot.A: Britain and Denmark were not poor members. They chose to stay out under special protocols.
whyNot.C: Both countries stayed in the EU. Britain left only in 2020, after a referendum.
whyNot.D: The regulation makes the euro the currency of the participating states. The pound and the krone were not part of it.

practice.hint: Britain and Denmark were among the richer members. Why might they still choose to stay out?

practice.stem: Which later development most clearly revealed a problem with sharing one currency?

options.A: the EU's admission of several former communist states in 2004
options.B: Britain's decision to leave the EU after its 2016 referendum
options.C: disputes over admitting refugees to EU states in 2015
options.D: the Greek debt crisis and rescue loans beginning in 2010

practice.explanation: Countries using the euro could no longer set their own interest rates or lower the value of their own money. In 2010 Greece could no longer borrow money at interest rates it could afford. In May 2010 it received rescue loans tied to harsh spending cuts. Ireland (2010) and Portugal (2011) also needed rescue loans.

whyNot.A: New members did not have to adopt the euro right away. Their joining the EU was not a problem caused by a shared currency.
whyNot.B: Britain kept the pound, so its decision to leave did not come from sharing the euro.
whyNot.C: These disputes were about migration and borders, not about a shared currency.

practice.hint: What does a country give up when it stops using its own currency?

practice.stem: The agreement Mowlam describes is best understood in the context of

options.A: the Irish War of Independence
options.B: the Troubles
options.C: the expulsion of Germans after 1945
options.D: the Cold War arms race

practice.explanation: From the late 1960s to the 1990s, about 3,500 people were killed in the conflict over Northern Ireland, most of them in Northern Ireland itself. Republican and loyalist armed groups and British security forces were involved. This period is called the Troubles. The Good Friday Agreement tried to end it.

whyNot.A: The Irish War of Independence ended in 1921. Mowlam speaks of violence that the agreement of 1998 was meant to end.
whyNot.C: The expulsion of Germans took place in Central Europe. It had nothing to do with Northern Ireland.
whyNot.D: The Cold War arms race was a contest between the superpowers. The Northern Ireland conflict was not part of it.

practice.hint: Mowlam mentions "the victims of violence." Which conflict had produced those victims?

practice.stem: According to Mowlam, the "principle of consent" means that

options.A: Northern Ireland stays in the United Kingdom unless most of its people choose otherwise
options.B: Northern Ireland will join the Republic of Ireland by the year 2000
options.C: Britain and Ireland will share equal control over the government of Northern Ireland
options.D: each community in Northern Ireland may veto any future vote on whether to leave the UK

practice.explanation: Under the principle of consent, Northern Ireland stays in the United Kingdom as long as most people there want that. If a majority ever votes for a united Ireland, Britain will act on that wish.

whyNot.B: The agreement sets no date for joining Ireland. A united Ireland would come only if a majority consented.
whyNot.C: Northern Ireland would be governed by its own assembly. The two governments would meet to discuss issues, but they would not share control.
whyNot.D: Under the principle of consent, a majority decides. No community has a veto over a vote on the border.

practice.hint: Reread the sentence that begins "First, on constitutional issues."

practice.stem: Which of the following most clearly distinguishes the peace process Mowlam describes from the settlements in Bosnia and Kosovo in the 1990s?

options.A: Outside governments played important roles in the talks.
options.B: The settlement tried to protect communities that had fought each other.
options.C: Negotiations helped set up a new way of governing the region.
options.D: An agreement was reached without NATO military intervention.

practice.explanation: The Good Friday Agreement came out of talks among the parties, and in May 1998 voters in both parts of Ireland approved it. In Bosnia (1995) and Kosovo (1999), peace came after NATO bombing as well as diplomacy.

whyNot.A: Outside governments helped in all three cases. In Northern Ireland, the former U.S. senator George Mitchell chaired the talks.
whyNot.B: All three settlements tried to protect communities that had been in conflict.
whyNot.C: All three settlements set up new ways of governing after talks.

practice.hint: How did the wars in Bosnia and Kosovo come to an end?

exam.title: Unit 9 Practice Exam: Cold War and Contemporary Europe
exam.directions: Each set of questions refers to a source: a primary source, a historian's writing, an image, or data. For each question, choose the best answer. Use the source and your knowledge of European history from c. 1914 to the present. There is no penalty for guessing. Some sources use historical labels or words for groups of people that are no longer used; these words show the language of their time.

questions.stem: The agreements in the passage are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: the Soviet blockade of West Berlin and the Western airlift that followed
options.B: debates over independence movements in the overseas empires of Britain and France
options.C: the victorious Allies' efforts to settle postwar Europe after Germany's defeat
options.D: the creation of the European Coal and Steel Community

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Berlin blockade began in 1948, three years after this agreement.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The passage is about Poland, Germany, and other states in Europe, not about colonies overseas.
rationales.C: Correct. In July and August 1945, the leaders of the Soviet Union, the United States, and Britain met at Potsdam, near Berlin, to decide the future of Germany and Eastern Europe.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Six Western European states signed the treaty creating the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951. It took effect in 1952, years after Potsdam.

questions.explanation: Germany surrendered in May 1945. At Potsdam, Stalin, Truman, and Britain's leaders (first Churchill, then Attlee) tried to settle the postwar order. Soviet armies already held most of Eastern Europe. The Western leaders asked for promises of free elections and a free press there, but they had little power to enforce them.

questions.stem: Which of the following later developments most clearly shows that the hopes for free elections and a free press expressed in the passage were not met?

options.A: Communist parties took over Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, and Poland by 1949.
options.B: Finland kept a democratic government after the war.
options.C: The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949.
options.D: Greece's government defeated communist rebels in a civil war that ended in 1949.

rationales.A: Correct. Poland's communists won rigged elections in 1947. Bulgaria's communists executed the opposition leader Nikola Petkov that year. Romania's king was forced to give up his throne that December. Hungary's communists pushed out their rivals by 1949.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Finland remained a parliamentary democracy after the war. That does not show that the freedoms promised in the passage were denied.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Soviet atomic bomb test in 1949 started a nuclear arms race. It had nothing to do with elections or a free press in the countries named in the passage.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Greece is not named in the passage, and its government defeated the communist rebels. Greece stayed out of the Soviet bloc.

questions.explanation: From 1945 to 1949, communist parties backed by the Soviet Union took power in Poland, Hungary, Romania, and Bulgaria. They used rigged elections, arrests, censorship, and threats. The promises made at Yalta and Potsdam were not kept.

questions.stem: The "transfer to Germany of German populations" described in the passage best illustrates which postwar development?

options.A: postwar ethnic cleansing
options.B: the return of Holocaust survivors
options.C: guest-worker recruitment
options.D: the flight of East Germans before 1961

rationales.A: Correct. Near the end of World War II and in the years after it, about 12 million Germans fled or were forced from their homes in Central and Eastern Europe. Many died. The expulsions targeted people because they were German. Driving out an ethnic group by force or threats is called ethnic cleansing.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The passage describes Germans being moved out of Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary, not Jewish survivors going home. Many survivors who tried to return home met hostility, and many left Eastern Europe.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Guest workers came to West Germany in the 1950s and 1960s to fill jobs. The passage describes Germans being forced out in 1945.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Millions of East Germans moved west before the Berlin Wall went up in 1961. The passage describes something else: Germans driven out of Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary.

questions.explanation: The passage asks Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary to "suspend further expulsions," which shows that Germans were already being driven out. The Allies said the transfers should be "orderly and humane." In fact, many expulsions were brutal, and many people died. It was one of the largest forced migrations in European history.

questions.stem: Attlee's description of the end of British rule in India was most likely intended to

options.A: persuade Parliament to keep British troops in India after independence
options.B: convince Indian leaders to give up the plan to partition India
options.C: present the end of British rule as an honorable choice, not a defeat
options.D: warn other colonial powers that they would soon lose their empires

rationales.A: Incorrect. Attlee says the new Dominions will be "completely free in all respects from any control by this country." He does not ask to keep troops there.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Attlee says that he and the Indian leaders "have had to accept" partition. The bill itself divided India into two Dominions.
rationales.C: Correct. Attlee says Britain chose to end its rule. He calls it "the fulfilment of Britain's mission," not "abdication." He was answering people who saw it as a loss.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Attlee notes that the demand for self-government "has spread throughout Asia." But he is speaking to Parliament about India. He is not warning other empires.

questions.explanation: Some members of Parliament, mostly Conservatives, saw the end of British India as a defeat. Attlee answered them. He called independence the completion of Britain's mission. He also said the new countries would gain from staying in the Commonwealth.

questions.stem: Which of the following would a historian most likely use to challenge Attlee's claim that British rule was ending "at the instance of this country"?

options.A: Britain's Labour Party had long promised India self-government.
options.B: Indian nationalist protests had made British rule very hard to keep.
options.C: India and Pakistan chose to stay in the Commonwealth after independence.
options.D: A 1935 British law gave India's provinces elected governments.

rationales.A: Incorrect. This fits Attlee's claim that ending British rule was Britain's own policy. It does not challenge it.
rationales.B: Correct. Gandhi and the Congress led mass campaigns, such as Quit India in 1942. In 1946 sailors of the Royal Indian Navy mutinied. Britain was also weak after the war. Many historians say Britain left because it could no longer hold India.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Staying in the Commonwealth fits Attlee's hopes for friendly ties. It says nothing about why Britain left.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The 1935 law fits Attlee's claim that self-government was Britain's "settled policy." It does not challenge it.

questions.explanation: Attlee says that Britain chose to leave. Many historians disagree. Years of Indian protest, unrest during the war, and Britain's lack of money after 1945 left Britain little choice.

questions.stem: The ties between Britain and the new Dominions that Attlee hoped would continue contributed most directly to which later development?

options.A: India's leading role in the Non-Aligned Movement
options.B: Indian and Pakistani support for Britain in the Suez Crisis of 1956
options.C: the wars between India and Pakistan over Kashmir
options.D: migration from India and Pakistan to Britain

rationales.A: Incorrect. India stayed in the Commonwealth, but it refused to join either side in the Cold War. Non-alignment came from India's own foreign policy, not from its ties with Britain.
rationales.B: Incorrect. When Britain and France attacked Egypt in 1956, India and Pakistan both voted at the United Nations for a ceasefire. The crisis divided the Commonwealth.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The fighting over Kashmir began in 1947. It grew out of partition and the dispute over which new country Kashmir would join, not out of ties with Britain.
rationales.D: Correct. The British Nationality Act of 1948 let citizens of Commonwealth countries, including India and Pakistan, enter Britain freely. Many came to fill jobs. The Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962 began to limit entry.

questions.explanation: India and Pakistan stayed in the Commonwealth. Under a 1948 law, their citizens could move to Britain freely. Many came to work in factories, in hospitals, and on buses and trains. Large South Asian communities grew in British cities.

questions.stem: In Source 1, Thatcher's main objection to plans for closer European union is that they would

options.A: end Britain's membership in the European Community
options.B: force Britain to accept refugees from Eastern Europe
options.C: require Britain to leave the NATO alliance
options.D: shift power from Parliament to European bodies

rationales.A: Incorrect. Thatcher says Britain fully accepts its "commitments under the treaties." She wants to "co-operate more closely" with the other members.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Thatcher does not mention refugees. She talks about the currency and about the powers of European bodies.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Thatcher does not mention NATO. Members of the European Community did not have to leave NATO.
rationales.D: Correct. Thatcher wants Britain to keep governing itself "through Parliament." She does not want the "non-elected" Commission to get more power.

questions.explanation: Thatcher supported cooperation and trade in the Community. But she opposed a single currency. She also opposed more power for the Commission and the European Parliament. She thought they would weaken the British Parliament.

questions.stem: Thatcher would most likely have objected to which of the following?

options.A: a single currency to replace national currencies
options.B: the end of the division between Eastern and Western Europe
options.C: decisions taken as closely as possible to the citizen
options.D: the admission of Spain and Portugal to the Community in 1986

rationales.A: Correct. Source 2 calls for "a single and stable currency." Thatcher says Britain would not give up "the pound sterling as our currency."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Thatcher's government welcomed the fall of communism. It supported aid to Eastern Europe's new democracies.
rationales.C: Incorrect. British leaders liked the idea that decisions should be made close to the citizen. It could limit the power of European bodies.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Spain and Portugal joined in 1986, while Thatcher was prime minister. Her government supported adding new members.

questions.explanation: Thatcher drew a line at the single currency. After she left office, her successor, John Major, won an opt-out at Maastricht. So Britain did not have to adopt the euro.

questions.stem: The reference in Source 2 to "the ending of the division of the European continent" is best understood in the context of

options.A: the defeat of Nazi Germany
options.B: the revolutions of 1989 and German reunification
options.C: the Helsinki Accords
options.D: Britain's entry into the European Community in 1973

rationales.A: Incorrect. The defeat of Germany in 1945 led to the division of Europe into East and West. It did not end it.
rationales.B: Correct. From 1989 to 1991, communist rule fell across Eastern Europe. Germany reunited in October 1990. Then the Soviet Union broke apart. The Cold War split of Europe was over.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Helsinki Accords of 1975 eased tensions. But they accepted Europe's borders, and the Cold War went on for fifteen more years.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Britain joined the European Community in 1973. That made the Community bigger in the West. It did not end the split between East and West.

questions.explanation: When the Maastricht Treaty was signed in February 1992, the Berlin Wall had fallen. Germany had reunited, and the Soviet Union had just broken up. The treaty's authors saw a chance to build a larger, closer union.

questions.stem: The disagreement shown in the two sources is most similar to which later development?

options.A: France's withdrawal from NATO's military command in 1966
options.B: Britain's 2016 referendum vote to leave the European Union, known as Brexit
options.C: the peaceful division of Czechoslovakia into two states in 1993
options.D: the European Union's expansion into Eastern Europe in 2004

rationales.A: Incorrect. De Gaulle took France out of NATO's military command in 1966. That was also about national independence. But it came before these sources, and it was about NATO, not European integration.
rationales.B: Correct. Many British voters still saw European integration as a threat to the power of Parliament. In June 2016 a majority of voters chose to leave the EU. Britain left in January 2020.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Czechs and Slovaks split peacefully in 1993. But the split was about their two nations, not about European integration.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The 2004 enlargement added ten new members. It made the EU bigger. It did not show a dispute over the EU's powers.

questions.explanation: Thatcher said Britain must keep the power to govern itself "through Parliament." Later critics of the European Union took up this argument. Their campaign led to the 2016 referendum and to Brexit.

questions.stem: The scene in the photograph is best understood in the context of

options.A: the forced labor of foreign workers in German factories during World War II
options.B: high unemployment in West Germany in the years just after the war
options.C: the flight of refugees from Hungary after the revolution of 1956
options.D: labor shortages during West Germany's postwar economic boom

rationales.A: Incorrect. The photograph was taken in 1962. Nazi forced labor ended in 1945. These women came under a peacetime recruitment deal.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Unemployment was high in West Germany around 1950. By 1962 there were more jobs than workers, so the government recruited workers abroad.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hungarian refugees went to many countries after 1956. But the archive says these women were guest workers from Italy.
rationales.D: Correct. In the boom of the 1950s and 1960s, West German factories needed more workers. The government signed deals to recruit them. It began with Italy in 1955, then Spain and Greece in 1960 and Turkey in 1961.

questions.explanation: West Germany's economy grew fast after 1950, and it needed more workers. From 1955 the government recruited guest workers from southern Europe and later from Turkey. The need grew after the Berlin Wall stopped East Germans from coming west in 1961.

questions.stem: Given its source and context, the photograph was most likely intended to

options.A: show foreign workers as a welcome part of the West German economy
options.B: warn West Germans that foreign workers were taking jobs away from Germans
options.C: persuade Italians working in West Germany to return home
options.D: criticize factory owners for paying foreign women low wages

rationales.A: Correct. The photograph was made for the West German government's press office. Its cheerful, orderly scene shows the recruiting of foreign workers as a success.
rationales.B: Incorrect. In 1962 West Germany had more jobs than workers. The government was busy recruiting foreign workers.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The government wanted the workers to stay and work. The smiling, busy women send no message to go home.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The photograph shows a clean, busy workplace and smiling workers. It gives no sign of low wages or of a complaint against the factory owners.

questions.explanation: Governments use photographs to shape opinion. This photo from the government's press office shows guest workers fitting in well. Later, after the slowdown of the 1970s, many guest workers faced hostility.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 calls on Czechoslovaks to resist the troops by force, while Source 2 calls for peaceful talks.
options.B: Source 1 blames the United States for the invasion, while Source 2 blames West Germany.
options.C: Source 1 says the troops came without its leaders' knowledge, while Source 2 says the government asked for them.
options.D: Source 1 announces that Czechoslovakia will leave the Warsaw Pact, while Source 2 demands that it stay in the alliance.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Source 1 says the party leaders told citizens "not to resist the advancing troops." Armed defense was impossible.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Source 1 names the troops of the Soviet Union and its allies, not the United States. Source 2 blames "imperialists" and "foreign powers hostile to socialism" without naming West Germany.
rationales.C: Correct. Source 1 says the invasion "happened without the knowledge" of the country's leaders. Source 2 claims the troops came "on the basis of a request by the Government of that State."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Unlike Hungary's Nagy in 1956, Dubček's government never said it would leave the Warsaw Pact. Source 1 does not say so either.

questions.explanation: Czechoslovakia's leaders said the invasion came without their knowledge and broke international law. The Soviet Union claimed that the government had asked for help. It had not. A few pro-Soviet party leaders had secretly written to Moscow, most famously in a letter signed by five of them.

questions.stem: The argument in the last paragraph of Source 2 is most closely associated with which of the following?

options.A: the Brezhnev Doctrine
options.B: the Truman Doctrine
options.C: de-Stalinization
options.D: the policy of peaceful coexistence

rationales.A: Correct. In late 1968 Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev said socialist countries had a duty to act when socialism was in danger in any one of them. Western writers called this the Brezhnev Doctrine.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Truman Doctrine of 1947 promised American help to countries resisting communist takeover. That was the opposite goal.
rationales.C: Incorrect. De-Stalinization was Khrushchev's attack on Stalin's crimes, starting in 1956. It was about Soviet policy at home, not a duty to step in abroad.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Peaceful coexistence was Khrushchev's idea that communist and capitalist states could compete without war. It did not justify invading allies.

questions.explanation: Malik says that defending "the socialist gains" of each country is a duty of "all the socialist States." This idea became known as the Brezhnev Doctrine. The Soviet Union used it to justify sending troops to keep communist parties in power.

questions.stem: The policy defended in Source 2 was abandoned when

options.A: Leonid Brezhnev died and Yuri Andropov took power in 1982
options.B: the superpowers signed the SALT I arms agreements in 1972
options.C: Gorbachev let Eastern European states go their own way in 1989
options.D: Poland's government declared martial law against Solidarity in 1981

rationales.A: Incorrect. Brezhnev died in November 1982, but Andropov and then Konstantin Chernenko kept the policy. Only Gorbachev gave it up.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The SALT I agreements of 1972 limited some nuclear weapons. They did not change Soviet control over Eastern Europe.
rationales.C: Correct. Gorbachev let the revolutions of 1989 happen without sending troops. A Soviet spokesman joked that the Brezhnev Doctrine had become the Sinatra Doctrine. Frank Sinatra sang the song My Way, and now each country could go its own way.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Martial law in Poland in 1981 crushed Solidarity under Soviet pressure. It continued the policy instead of ending it.

questions.explanation: In 1989 Gorbachev needed to cut costs and improve ties with the West. He refused to use force to save the communist governments of Eastern Europe. One after another they fell, and the Soviet bloc came to an end.

questions.stem: During the period 1950 to 1970, the major factor explaining the trend in France and Italy was

options.A: wealth flowing back to Europe from colonies after decolonization
options.B: central planning of the economy modeled on the Soviet Union
options.C: rebuilding, cheap oil, and freer trade in the Common Market
options.D: high oil prices that brought profits to European oil exporters

rationales.A: Incorrect. Decolonization ended Europe's control of its colonies' wealth. Italy had lost its colonies after World War II.
rationales.B: Incorrect. France and Italy had market economies. France did some planning, but not Soviet-style central planning.
rationales.C: Correct. GDP per person in France more than doubled. In Italy it nearly tripled. Rebuilding after the war, cheap oil, and the Common Market of 1957 all helped both economies grow fast.
rationales.D: Incorrect. France and Italy imported most of their oil. Oil was cheap until 1973, and that helped them grow.

questions.explanation: Western Europe's boom lasted from about 1950 to the early 1970s. Rebuilding, American aid, cheap oil, and freer trade in the Common Market all helped these economies grow fast.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the period from 1980 to 1989 is best supported by the data?

options.A: Poland's GDP per person grew faster than that of any other country shown.
options.B: The gap between the Western and the communist countries grew.
options.C: GDP per person in the Soviet Union fell below its 1970 level.
options.D: The communist countries caught up with Britain by the end of the decade.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Poland's figures for 1980 and 1989 both round to $9,100, so it barely changed. That was the weakest record in the table.
rationales.B: Correct. In 1980 France was about $14,400 ahead of Poland. By 1989 it was about $18,500 ahead. Britain's lead over the Soviet Union grew from about $10,400 to about $14,900.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Soviet figure rose from $8,900 in 1970 to $11,300 in 1989.
rationales.D: Incorrect. In 1989 Britain's figure was $26,200. That was higher than the figure for any communist country shown.

questions.explanation: In the 1980s the Western economies grew. The communist economies grew slowly, and Poland's GDP per person barely changed. This slowdown helped lead to Gorbachev's reforms and to the fall of communism in Eastern Europe in 1989.

questions.stem: The slower growth shown for France and Italy after 1970 was part of a wider slowdown in Western Europe in the 1970s. That slowdown contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: the creation of Britain's National Health Service
options.B: the founding of the European Coal and Steel Community
options.C: the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979
options.D: criticism of high taxes and welfare spending

rationales.A: Incorrect. The National Health Service began in 1948. That was before the slowdown, not after it.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Coal and Steel Community was founded in 1951, during the years of fast growth.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan came from the Soviet wish to keep a communist government in power there, not from slower growth in Western Europe.
rationales.D: Correct. In the 1970s growth slowed and prices rose. Government budgets came under strain. Conservative leaders such as Margaret Thatcher, prime minister from 1979, blamed high taxes and a large welfare state.

questions.explanation: The postwar boom had paid for generous welfare programs. Growth slowed after the oil shock of 1973. Critics on the right then called for lower taxes and a smaller state. Some governments cut spending.

questions.stem: The "ethnic cleansing" described in the passage is best understood in the context of

options.A: the breakup of Yugoslavia
options.B: the expulsion of Germans after 1945
options.C: the Hungarian Revolution of 1956
options.D: the Soviet war in Afghanistan

rationales.A: Correct. After communism fell, Yugoslavia split along national lines. Serb, Croat, and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) nationalists fought over Bosnia. Bosnian Serb forces drove out and killed Bosnian Muslims to build a "Greater Serbia."
rationales.B: Incorrect. The expulsion of Germans took place in 1945–1950. The passage describes Bosnia in the 1990s.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Soviet troops crushed Hungary's revolt in 1956. It was a fight against Soviet rule, not a fight between ethnic groups.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Soviet war in Afghanistan (1979–1989) took place in Central Asia. It ended before the war in Bosnia began.

questions.explanation: Yugoslavia broke apart in 1991 and 1992. In the war in Bosnia (1992 to 1995), Bosnian Serb forces drove out and killed Bosnian Muslims. In July 1995 they killed about 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica. International courts later called it genocide.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most important for a historian to consider when using the passage as evidence about the fall of Srebrenica?

options.A: It was written about four years after the fall of Srebrenica.
options.B: It discusses the war in Kosovo as well as the war in Bosnia.
options.C: It was written in English, not in a language of the former Yugoslavia.
options.D: Its UN authors were judging their own organization's failures.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Four years is a short time. Many witnesses and records were still available when the report was written.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Mentioning Kosovo widens the report's lesson. It does not limit the report's value as evidence about Srebrenica.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The language of the report does not change its point of view. What matters most is that the UN was judging its own actions.
rationales.D: Correct. The report was written by the UN's own leaders. It openly admits "error" and "misjudgement." A historian should still compare it with other sources, such as court records and survivors' accounts.

questions.explanation: Kofi Annan's report is unusual. In it, an organization judges its own mistakes. That makes it valuable. But the authors' point of view still shapes which failures they stress.

questions.stem: The report's conclusion that an attempt "to terrorize, expel or murder an entire people must be met decisively" most clearly reflects lessons drawn from which earlier event?

options.A: the Hungarian Revolution of 1956
options.B: the Holocaust during the Second World War
options.C: the Reign of Terror during the French Revolution
options.D: the Russian Civil War after 1917

rationales.A: Incorrect. In 1956 Soviet troops crushed a political revolt in Hungary. It was not an attempt to destroy a whole people.
rationales.B: Correct. After the Nazis murdered six million Jews, the UN adopted the Genocide Convention in 1948. Many Europeans vowed that such crimes must never happen again. The report applies that lesson to Bosnia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Reign of Terror (1793–1794) executed people seen as enemies of the Revolution. It was political repression, not an attempt to destroy a people.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Russian Civil War was a fight for power between the Reds and the Whites. It was not the event that made genocide a lesson for postwar Europe.

questions.explanation: The memory of the Holocaust shaped postwar ideas about human rights and genocide. Many Europeans were shocked that genocide could happen in Europe again in the 1990s.

questions.stem: The ban on reproductive cloning in Article 3 is best understood in the context of

options.A: the development of the birth control pill in the 1950s and 1960s
options.B: advances in genetics, such as the birth of Dolly the sheep
options.C: the discovery of penicillin in the 1920s
options.D: the spread of the AIDS epidemic in the 1980s

rationales.A: Incorrect. The pill prevents pregnancy. It does not make a genetic copy of a person.
rationales.B: Correct. In 1996 scientists in Scotland cloned a sheep, Dolly, from an adult cell. Her birth was announced in 1997. Many people feared that human cloning would follow.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Penicillin treats infections caused by bacteria. It does not copy genetic material.
rationales.D: Incorrect. AIDS raised concerns about public health and unfair treatment, not about cloning human beings.

questions.explanation: New genetic and medical tools raised hard moral questions. People of different beliefs did not agree about them. Article 3 bans the reproductive cloning of human beings. It also bans eugenic practices, which recall Nazi Germany's efforts to control who could have children.

questions.stem: The inclusion of "sexual orientation" in Article 21 most directly reflects

options.A: the teachings of the Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council
options.B: the influence of Soviet law on the European Union
options.C: new laws against homosexuality passed in Western Europe in the 1990s
options.D: campaigns by gay and lesbian movements for equal rights

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) changed Catholic worship and ties with other faiths. It did not call for laws against discrimination based on sexual orientation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. In 1934 Soviet law made sexual relations between men a crime. That law lasted until after the Soviet Union ended.
rationales.C: Incorrect. In the 1990s Western European countries were removing laws against homosexuality. They were not passing new ones.
rationales.D: Correct. After the 1960s, gay and lesbian groups campaigned against unfair treatment. Denmark created registered partnerships for same-sex couples in 1989. In 2001 the Netherlands became the first country to allow same-sex marriage.

questions.explanation: After the 1960s, gay and lesbian groups, like women's groups, campaigned for equal rights. By 2000 several Western European countries had passed laws to protect gay and lesbian people. These groups also faced strong opposition.

questions.stem: The inclusion of Article 37 in the Charter most directly reflects

options.A: social democratic campaigns to expand public welfare
options.B: conservative campaigns to reduce state regulation

rationales.A: Incorrect. These campaigns were about pensions, health care, and other public services. Article 37 is about the environment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. These campaigns wanted fewer rules. Article 37 asks for more protection of the environment.
rationales.C: Correct. Green parties, such as West Germany's Greens, challenged consumerism and called for sustainable development. Fears about acid rain, nuclear accidents, and climate change made the environment a European issue.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Lower trade barriers help trade between countries. Article 37 is about protecting nature.

questions.explanation: From the 1970s on, Green parties and environmental groups pushed governments to protect nature. By 2000 the European Union treated sustainable development as a basic rule.

questions.stem: The second sentence of Article 23 would most likely be used to defend

options.A: parity rules for women and men on party candidate lists
options.B: laws guaranteeing equal pay for women and men doing the same work
options.C: the right of women to vote in national and local elections
options.D: the legalization of divorce in Italy in 1970

rationales.A: Correct. The second sentence allows "specific advantages" for the sex with fewer seats or jobs. For example, a 2000 French law made parties run as many women as men in many elections.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Equal pay is covered by the first sentence ("employment, work and pay"). The second sentence is about special advantages.
rationales.C: Incorrect. By 2000 women could vote in every EU member state. Voting rights do not give "specific advantages" to one sex.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Italy's 1970 divorce law gave new rights to both spouses. It did not give special advantages to one sex.

questions.explanation: Women held few seats in most European parliaments in the 1990s. The second sentence of Article 23 allows special steps, such as quotas or parity rules. They help the sex that has fewer seats or jobs.
